title: AA Batteries 8-pack

drivers.name: 10% off promotion
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted uplift of x1.17 from 7 past promotions; consistent with price drop of 5.1% and 10% discount depth.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 34.8. Thanksgiving historically lifts sales to x1.4 vs baseline, but the noise-adjusted estimate is x1.0—indicating the effect is unreliable and likely due to noise. The 10% off promotion has a noise-adjusted uplift of x1.17 from 7 past instances. The price drop is 5.1%, consistent with prior promotions. The classical model suggests 1.17, but this combines a weak holiday effect (x1.0) and a solid promotion effect (x1.17). No double-counting: the promotion is the main driver. The downside spread remains 1.0 (no supply or demand risk). The upside spread increases slightly to 1.15 due to uncertainty in the promotion's full impact, though evidence is moderate. Confidence is medium due to limited reliable holiday data.

TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-23 to 2026-11-29 (7 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Thanksgiving (Thu); Promotion: 10% off, featured in weekly ad
  shelf price: 9.73 (-5.1% vs regular price 10.25)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 34.8 | 5%-95%: 17.9 - 58.9 | 10%-90%: 20.3 - 55.7

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-44% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
